title: Nat Alison: Procedurality and the Primes
speaker: Nat Alison
summary: Nat Alison, a math designer at Uma Games and mathematical visualization artist, argues playfully that 'math is a roguelike': the same three qualities that make procedural generation interesting also make mathematics interesting. Those are complexity emerging from simple rules (axioms, group theory, the natural numbers and primes), a balance between order and chaos (Perlin noise, the Ulam spiral, prime and coprime visualizations), and surprise and joy of discovery (Euler's identity, her Fibonacci-modulus plots). She notes the balance decays as patterns become rote and can be restored by self-imposed challenges, and closes by urging procedural developers to study the math tools they use for their own sake.

insights.claim: Procedural generation is interesting when it produces complexity from simple rules, balances order and chaos, and yields surprise and joy.
insights.detail: Alison proposes these three criteria for what makes procedurality compelling, contrasting good output with mere 'content oatmeal or alphabet soup'. Her thesis is that the same three criteria are what make mathematics interesting, hence 'math is a roguelike'.
insights.quote: This idea of complexity from simplicity and taking simple rules and getting way more complex out of it. Having a balance of order and chaos

insights.claim: Procedural generation typically uses mathematics as a tool to produce a picture or world, whereas pure math studies the underlying model itself, and generator makers can benefit from the latter view.
insights.detail: Alison distinguishes the familiar 'roguelikes are math' from her claim 'math is a roguelike'. Developers use fractals or noise because they produce a cool image or fun world; mathematicians are interested in why the model behaves as it does. Her closing exercise asks developers to prod their tools, e.g. when a cellular automaton leads to interesting results, or what game-theory strategy a deckbuilder run converges on.
insights.quote: You are using the mathematics a as a tool and interested into tool of a picture or a game world that's fun to traverse.

insights.claim: A small set of rules can generate an entire universe of structure, as in L-systems, Tracery grammars, and mathematical axioms such as group theory or the natural numbers.
insights.detail: Alison links procedural techniques like string-rewriting trees and Tracery bots to axioms in math. Rubik's cube moves, rotations of a tetrahedron and card permutations all obey shared group rules, and abstracting them yields a zoo of symmetries, including 'sporadic groups' with no real-world equivalent. Defining counting, addition and multiplication leads to primes and an endless well of theory.
insights.quote: this core of taking some sort of small set of rules, and seeing what comes out of them is true in math as well. In math these are called axioms.

insights.claim: Go shows how a deep metagame and rich vocabulary can emerge from very simple placement and capture rules, which Alison uses as an analogy for apparent complexity in mathematics.
insights.detail: Answering the counterclaim that math is just complicated jargon, Alison notes that Go's rules are simple but thousands of years of play built a complex theory and vocabulary on top of them. Similarly, mathematical complexity is emergence from rules as basic as counting.
insights.quote: Go has a simple rule. You take turns placing stones on the grid.

insights.claim: Generated output is most engaging when it sits between order and chaos, because full symmetry is boring and full randomness is intractable, while near-patterns make the mind search for structure.
insights.detail: Alison compares a uniform grid, white noise and Perlin noise; Perlin noise sits in between and feels naturalistic, which is one reason it is used for terrain. Even numbers are boring, random lists are boring, but primes have almost-visible patterns (twin primes, the Ulam spiral's diagonals), which keeps people needling at them.
insights.quote: Complete symmetry is boring whereas complete chaos is in tractable.

insights.claim: Alison's prime and coprime visualizations (a 'modular mandala' and 'prime logs') show patterns that are locally regular yet hard to predict globally, illustrating the order-chaos balance.
insights.detail: In the modular mandala each strand marks numbers coprime to a given number; each strand repeats clearly but successive strands are hard to predict, yet they sometimes all line up. The prime logs stack log-scaled prime factors, which look random until structure appears where small primes intersect.
insights.quote: If you look at each strand, you can see a clear repeating pattern like dot dot blank and so on.

insights.claim: The order-chaos balance of a roguelike erodes with repeated play as strategies become rote and generated content blends into noise.
insights.detail: Alison describes settling on a favourite deck in a game and then getting bored once she learned its strategies: the chaos becomes tame and 'the trees all start looking the same'. She draws a parallel to large primes, which are hard to tell apart compared to small numbers like two and three.
insights.quote: You learn strategies and the chaos becomes team and the patterns are wrote. The trees all start looking the same.

insights.claim: Players can restore a stale game's balance through self-imposed challenge runs, speedrunning and mods, which amend existing content to find something new.
insights.detail: Alison offers these as the fix to rote play, and draws the parallel that mathematicians make large numbers interesting by finding special classes like Mersenne or Fibonacci primes. In both, you can 'carve out your own path and find the fun yourself'.
insights.quote: In roguelikes you can do challenge runs. Self-imposed challenges, speed running, mods, there are a lot of ways where you can amend the current content

insights.claim: Procedural generation succeeds best when it creates surprisingly poignant, beautiful or funny results, like the sense in Slay the Spire that the stars are aligning and you are somehow cheating.
insights.detail: Alison names surprise and joy as the third criterion. She compares a synergy moment in Slay the Spire to Euler's identity, where unrelated constants combine to equal zero and it feels magical.
insights.quote: Proc gen succeeds best when you create things that are surprising. Things that are surprisingly poignant or beautiful and funny.

insights.claim: Discoveries that first seem like flukes feel rewarding when players learn they were intended, as with synergies developers deliberately place for players to find.
insights.detail: Alison raises the worry that a striking pattern is just coincidence, like the golden spiral overlaid on everything. She notes that roguelike synergies were planned all along by developers, and that in math, magical-seeming results become as natural as 1+1=2 once studied, as she found by researching her Fibonacci plots.
insights.quote: Game developers intended for you to find those synergize.

insights.claim: Plotting pairs of Fibonacci remainders for different moduli produced unexpected recurring cross and fractal patterns, an example of a simple generative experiment yielding surprising output.
insights.detail: Alison took Fibonacci numbers modulo various bases, plotted successive pairs on a grid, and found hashtag-like crosses (for modulus 89) and varied intricate shapes for 90, 98, 102 and 125. She later found the cross appears whenever the modulus is itself a Fibonacci number, and multiples of five give long periods, linking to the golden ratio.
insights.quote: I just decided to take pairs of them and plot them into grid and see what happens

insights.claim: Alison's educational sandbox game aims to teach math as reasoning, deduction and the joy of discovery rather than memorization.
insights.detail: As 'math designer' at Uma Games on Project Marble, a sandbox for young players, she designs systems and puzzles to show math is fun. She argues the joy of discovery, treading your own path and mastering it, is at the heart of mathematics, with proof as a tool for that discovery, and that is what the game tries to teach.
insights.quote: This joy of discovery is kind of at the heart of mathematics. Treading a path of your own and mastering it. It isn't memorizing
